hints: Notice the dashed box shows the cell $E$ in series with its internal resistance $r$, and the same current $I$ flows through $r$ and the external resistor $R$.
Recall the two $IR$-type terms: terminal p.d. across $R$ is $IR$ and voltage lost inside the cell is $Ir$.
Think how $E$ splits around the single loop, then rearrange $E = Ir + IR$ to match one of the given forms with $E - Ir$ on the left.
walkthrough: Identify the loop: current $I$ from the cell passes in series through internal resistance $r$ and external resistance $R$, as shown in the diagram.
State the conservation of energy rule for a complete circuit: e.m.f. equals sum of p.d.s around the loop, so $E = V_r + V_R$.
Use $V = IR$ for each resistor: voltage lost inside is $V_r = Ir$ and terminal p.d. across the load is $V_R = IR$, giving $E = Ir + IR$.
Rearrange by subtracting the internal drop from both sides: $E - Ir = IR$, which shows terminal p.d. is less than e.m.f. when current flows.

options.A: The e.m.f. $E$ minus the lost volts $Ir$ in internal resistance $r$ leaves the terminal p.d. $IR$ across $R$.
options.B: This subtracts $IR$ from $Ir$, which would make $E$ smaller than the internal drop and reverses the sign of the external p.d.
options.C: This adds $Ir$ to $E$, which would imply the terminal p.d. is larger than the e.m.f., impossible for a cell supplying current.
options.D: This omits the internal resistance $r$ and would only be true for an ideal cell with $r = 0$.
